title: Val Camonica: 300,000 petroglyphs, 8000 BCE-19th c.
summary: Europe's largest petroglyph collection, Lombardy Italy; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979 (Italy's first). Iron Age panels (~1st millennium BCE) include humanoid figures nicknamed 'the astronauts' for their rounded heads and radiating lines.

title: Camunian rose and the astronauts: ideograms, not spacesuits
summary: Archaeologist Emmanuel Anati, who led the decades-long survey, reads the horned/haloed humanoids and the spiral Camunian rose (nine cupmarks in a meander) as solar/religious ideograms tied to Iron Age Camunni ritual life, not literal equipment.

title: Astronauts of Val Camonica: the ancient-astronaut reading
summary: Ancient-astronaut writers, following Erich von Daniken's genre, point to the rounded helmet-like outlines and radiating lines around some figures as suits and antennae, naming the panels alongside Nazca and Palenque as evidence of prehistoric contact.

title: What's genuinely odd at Val Camonica
summary: The helmet-like outlines are real and the site spans 10,000+ years of continuous carving, so some figures read as more ambiguous than others; the fair-reader takeaway is that a handful of Iron Age panels sustain the reading, not that the ambiguity favors it.

title: Val Camonica: what would settle it
summary: A full contextual re-survey tying each astronaut panel to its surrounding Iron Age ritual scenes (weapons, plowing, dancing) would show whether the helmet figures cluster with mundane ceremonial imagery or stand apart -- so far they cluster.

title: Wandjina: Kimberley rock art, still a living tradition
summary: Thousands of Wandjina figures -- pale, mouthless, halo-headed beings -- are painted across Kimberley (Western Australia) rock shelters; the Worrora, Ngarinyin and Wunambal peoples still repaint them on a ritual cycle to keep their power active.

title: Wandjina in Aboriginal cosmology: creator-spirits, not visitors
summary: Traditional owners describe Wandjina as supreme creator beings who made the country and gave the law; the mouthless face and radiating headdress read, in-culture, as lightning and cloud imagery tied to the wet-season rains, not breathing gear.

title: Wandjina as Greys: the ancient-astronaut reading
summary: Erich von Daniken's 1968 Chariots of the Gods? proposed the figures depict extraterrestrial visitors; the resemblance of the round heads and huge black eyes to the popular Grey alien image has kept the claim circulating on UFO sites since.

title: Traditional owners call the alien theory harmful, not just wrong
summary: Worrora woman Leah Umbagai says the alien reading feels like being told they're making things up about a living religion; the fair-reader point is that this isn't a neutral puzzle -- it's someone else's sacred imagery being relabeled without consultation.

title: Wandjina: what would settle it
summary: An 1837 sketch by explorer George Grey circulated in Britain and picked up otherworldly framing well before von Daniken; tracing that publication history further would confirm the alien reading as a 19th-20th c. outsider projection, not a gap in the archaeology.

title: Sego Canyon: Barrier Canyon and Fremont rock art, Utah
summary: Sego Canyon panels layer three traditions: Archaic-period (8000-500 BCE) Barrier Canyon Style limbless, hollow-eyed anthropomorphs up to 9 feet tall, plus later Fremont (600-1250 CE) and historic Ute figures painted on the same sandstone wall.

title: Archaeologists: shamanic vision imagery, not visitors
summary: The armless torsos, vacant or bug eyes, and vertical body markings are read by archaeologists as entoptic/shamanic imagery tied to ritual and hallucinogen use -- a Barrier Canyon style attested across the Colorado Plateau well before any Fremont or Hopi presence.

title: Ancient Aliens on Sego Canyon; the Blue Star Kachina prophecy
summary: History Channel's Ancient Aliens (Giorgio Tsoukalos) frames Sego Canyon's ghostly figures as a visitation record; parallel claims read the Hopi Blue Star Kachina (Saquasohuh) prophecy -- a being appearing in the sky heralding the Fifth World -- as forecasting a real celestial or alien event.

title: The Blue Star Kachina prophecy is the odd part -- but not for the reason claimed
summary: Researcher Jason Colavito traced the popular Blue Star Kachina prophecy text and found no version predating the late 20th century -- the oddity isn't ancient sky-beings, it's a modern prophecy text retrofitted onto real Hopi katsina tradition and then read as corroboration.

title: Hopi/Anasazi star-beings: what would settle it
summary: For Sego Canyon, style-dating already places Barrier Canyon imagery millennia before Hopi culture existed, which is close to dispositive; for the Blue Star Kachina, publishing the earliest documented source of the prophecy text (versus its claimed oral-tradition origin) would settle whether it predates 20th-century channeling literature.

title: The Saqqara Bird: a carved wooden object, Ptolemaic Egypt
summary: A sycamore-wood object, 15cm long with an 18.3cm wingspan, found in 1898 in the tomb of Pa-di-Imen at Saqqara and dated to roughly 200 BCE; painted to resemble a falcon and held today in the Cairo Egyptian Museum.

title: Mainstream reading: a bird-shaped mast-head or votive object
summary: Egyptologists classify it as a bird figurine, most likely a ship's mast-head ornament or ritual/votive object common to the period; no ancient Egyptian aircraft or aviation text has ever been found to corroborate a functional role.

title: Dr. Khalil Messiha: a model glider
summary: Physician Khalil Messiha, who catalogued the piece in 1969, argued its vertical (not horizontal) tail fin and legless, high-lift wing profile mimic aerodynamic design rather than a real bird's anatomy, and proposed it was a scale model of a known aircraft or glider.

title: The aerodynamic tests genuinely disagree
summary: Replica tests split: Messiha's balsa copy reportedly glided; aviation engineer Martin Gregorie called the original totally unstable without a tailplane; a 2006 wind-tunnel replica without the tail still produced meaningful lift. That's real, unresolved engineering disagreement -- it just doesn't reach ancient aircraft, since no full-scale wreck or written reference exists.

title: Saqqara Bird: what would settle it
summary: A controlled wind-tunnel comparison against real falcon mast-head figurines from the same period and workshop would show whether the tail fin is a design choice unique to this piece or normal variation in bird-figurine carving -- that comparison hasn't been published.

title: The Dendera reliefs: crypt carvings at the Temple of Hathor
summary: Carved in underground crypts of the Hathor Temple at Dendera (Ptolemaic/Roman era, roughly 54 BCE-68 CE), the reliefs show an oval bulb-like shape containing a snake, flanked by Djed-pillar arms and a kneeling figure.

title: Egyptologists: Harsomtus emerging from a lotus, not a lamp
summary: The oval is the hn-vessel likened to the womb of the sky goddess Nut; the snake is the god Harsomtus (sometimes merged with Ra) being born from a lotus flower -- a standard creation/resurrection motif, with the Djed pillar (stability) and serpent iconography attested identically elsewhere in Egyptian temple art without any bulb.

title: The Dendera Light: an ancient electric lamp
summary: A Norwegian engineer first floated an electric-lamp reading; Austrian authors Peter Krassa and Rainer Habeck popularized it in a dedicated book, following Erich von Daniken's broader ancient-high-technology framing, reading the oval as a bulb, the snake as a filament, and the supports as a cable.

title: Why archaeologists treat this one as closed, not just disputed
summary: Archaeologist Kenneth Feder's rebuttal is a clean falsification test: an operating bulb-and-wiring technology used across a temple complex for centuries should leave sockets, glass shards, filament wire, or soot patterns proving its absence elsewhere -- none exist, and Dendera's own walls carry ordinary soot-blackened lamp niches.

title: Dendera: what would settle it
summary: It is already close to settled by the absence of any supporting material culture (wiring, batteries, bulbs) anywhere in the Egyptian record; the remaining open thread is purely historiographic -- dating the Norwegian engineer's original publication to pin down when the lamp reading entered circulation.

title: Pacal's sarcophagus lid, Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque
summary: The carved limestone lid covers the tomb of K'inich Janaab' Pakal (603-683 CE), ruler of Palenque, discovered in 1952; it shows a reclining figure at the base of a cross-shaped world tree topped by a bird.

title: Maya epigraphy: death and rebirth through the World Tree
summary: Deciphered Maya iconography reads the panel as Pakal falling into the underworld at death and rising toward the heavens via the World Tree, flanked by the Celestial Bird above and the Sun Monster/underworld jaws below; the controls are stylized hand gestures, the exhaust is the tree's roots, and the breathing tube is a funerary bone nose-ornament.

title: Von Daniken's astronaut-in-a-rocket reading
summary: Erich von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods? (1968) described the panel as a man operating a rocket's controls, leaning forward with an oxygen hose, flames issuing from an exhaust -- arguing that primitive imagination could not have invented an image so similar to a modern spacecraft.

title: Mayanists call this the clearest case of the genre
summary: Because Classic Maya writing on the tomb names Pakal and dates his death, and the World Tree motif recurs on dozens of other Maya monuments needing no machine reading, specialists treat the rocket claim as demonstrating the argument's method -- pattern-matching to modern technology while ignoring available text -- more than as a live debate.

title: Pacal: what would settle it
summary: It is effectively settled by the deciphered glyphs naming Pakal and his lineage directly on the lid; the honest open question is rhetorical rather than evidentiary -- why the rocket reading still circulates decades after Maya script became broadly readable in the 1980s-90s.

title: Madonna with Saint Giovannino: a 15th-century Florentine panel
summary: Attributed to Domenico Ghirlandaio's workshop, the panel (now in Florence's Palazzo Vecchio, Loeser collection) shows Mary, the Christ child and young John the Baptist, with a small glowing disc trailing light in the upper-right sky, and a man and dog below looking up at it.

title: Art history: a luminous cloud, standard Nativity iconography
summary: Shepherds shielding their eyes while gazing at a glowing cloud, often with an angel inside, is a recurring convention in 14th-16th c. Italian religious painting; the Nativity Star is depicted separately at left in the same panel, showing the artist deliberately distinguished the two symbols.

title: UFOlogy: a disc-shaped craft caught mid-flight
summary: UFO researchers since the 1980s cite the painting, alongside similar objects in other period frescoes such as Visoki Decani monastery, as pictorial evidence of anomalous aerial craft witnessed by medieval and Renaissance observers and folded into devotional scenes.

title: The genre problem: dozens of glowing-cloud paintings, one gets singled out
summary: The UFO reading survives mainly because this one panel circulates without its companions; compared against contemporaneous shepherd-and-cloud scenes, the composition stops looking anomalous and starts looking like a well-attested visual formula, which is the fair-reader's real takeaway.

title: Renaissance UFO paintings: what would settle it
summary: A published side-by-side catalog of the glowing-cloud-with-onlookers motif across dated Italian panels (several already identified) would let anyone check whether Giovannino's sky-object is stylistically identical to unambiguous angel-in-cloud scenes -- informally it already looks that way.

title: The Nazca lines: geoglyphs, 500 BCE-500 CE
summary: Made by removing dark surface pebbles to expose lighter soil, the geoglyphs cover the Nazca desert (southern Peru) with geometric lines and animal/plant figures, built in two phases by the Paracas (c. 400-200 BCE) and Nazca (200 BCE-500 CE) cultures using simple stakes and cords.

title: Leading scholarly theories: water, ritual, astronomy -- walked, not flown
summary: Maria Reiche and Paul Kosok proposed astronomical alignments; Johan Reinhard reads the lines as ritual paths to water-linked shrines; Donald Proulx and Stephen Mabee tie them to groundwater sources -- all converge on the lines being walked as pilgrimage or ceremonial routes, meant to be experienced from the ground, not viewed from above.

title: Von Daniken: landing strips for ancient astronauts
summary: Erich von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods? proposed the lines were built as runways or landing markers for extraterrestrial craft, an idea that reached mass audiences and remains the most widely known explanation for the lines outside archaeology.

title: Reiche's rebuttal and Nickell's replication both cut deep
summary: Maria Reiche, who spent decades surveying the lines, called the landing-strip idea absurd on its face since the ground is too soft to land anything on; skeptic Joe Nickell then had a small team reproduce a large figure in days using period tools, converting who else could have done this from a rhetorical question into a tested claim.

title: Nazca: what would settle it
summary: The intended-audience question is real and still open even without aliens -- whether the lines were meant to be seen by gods or ancestors from the sky, walked by pilgrims, or both; further excavation at line intersections, where smashed ceremonial pottery has already been found, bears more directly on that than any aerial-view argument does.

title: Dogon Sirius mystery: Griaule and Dieterlen's 1930s-1950s Mali fieldwork
summary: French ethnographers Marcel Griaule and Germaine Dieterlen worked with the Dogon of Mali from the 1930s to 1956 and reported that Dogon cosmology (via informant Ogotemmeli) described Sirius as a double star with a dense, invisible companion -- a claim with no telescopic possibility for a pre-contact society, later popularized by Robert Temple as evidence of alien contact.

title: Van Beek's 1991 Dogon restudy found no independent knowledge of Sirius B
summary: Anthropologist Walter van Beek returned to the Dogon in 1991 specifically to check Griaule's claim and found that knowledge of the stars held little importance in Dogon ritual life; no informant, including Griaule's own original sources, had heard of Sirius as a double star -- several said they had learned it from Griaule himself.

title: Robert Temple: aliens from Sirius taught the Dogon their astronomy
summary: Temple's 1976 The Sirius Mystery argues the Dogon's claimed knowledge could only have come from beings native to the Sirius system who visited Earth and 'taught the arts of civilization' -- built entirely on Griaule and Dieterlen's field reports, with no independent verification of Dogon astronomical knowledge before their arrival.

title: Which mundane channel explains Dogon 'Sirius' knowledge is itself unsettled
summary: Aliens are not a live option, but the exact leak is: Carl Sagan pointed to French astronomers who camped in West Africa for an 1893 eclipse expedition and to widespread 1920s newspaper coverage of Sirius B; others suspect Griaule's own leading interview style planted the idea in his informants. Both explain the outcome; neither has been nailed down as the specific channel.

title: Emerald Tablets of Thoth: a claimed 1925 Giza find, actually first published in the 1940s
summary: Maurice Doreal claimed to have found and translated ancient emerald tablets belonging to Thoth during a 1925 trip to Giza. The text was not published until the 1940s or early 1950s -- a 15-25 year gap between the claimed discovery and any public trace of the material, with no original tablet ever produced.

title: Colavito: the Emerald Tablets directly copy Lovecraft and Frank Belknap Long
summary: Researcher Jason Colavito documents passages in Doreal's Emerald Tablets of Thoth lifted close to verbatim from H.P. Lovecraft's The Dunwich Horror (1929) and Long's The Hounds of Tindalos (1929) -- weird fiction published in the same years Doreal was supposedly still sitting on an untranslated ancient manuscript.

title: Kolbrin Bible's claimed origin: 3,600-year-old texts saved from an 1184 Glastonbury fire
summary: The Kolbrin presents itself as eleven ancient Egyptian and Celtic manuscripts, rescued by monks from a real 1184 fire at Glastonbury Abbey and kept hidden for eight centuries before surfacing in the 1990s -- a chain-of-custody story with no monastery record, no intermediate owner, and no manuscript ever shown to a scholar.

title: Kolbrin's actual paper trail starts in 1992, not 1184
summary: The Culdian Trust published the Kolbrin in New Zealand in 1994, saying an unnamed 'elderly man' from the defunct Hope Trust had produced the current text around 1992 from unspecified originals never preserved or examined. A US edition (2005-2006) briefly inserted the modern term 'Nibiru' into the supposedly ancient text before quietly removing it.

title: Kolbrin echoes a real 18th-century British precedent for manufactured antiquity
summary: The name Kolbrin recalls Coelbren y Beirdd, an alphabet the Welsh poet Iolo Morganwg invented and presented as ancient Druidic writing in the 1790s-1820s. The parallel is suggestive rather than proven, but it places the Kolbrin inside a documented tradition of British antiquarian forgery rather than a unique mystery.

title: One recency signature, four traditions: Blue Star Kachina, Dogon Sirius, Emerald Tablets, Kolbrin
summary: Each case follows the same shape: a claim of deep antiquity, a documentable first appearance clustered in the 20th century, and content that mirrors sources available right around that first appearance (1920s astronomy news, 1920s weird fiction, 1990s New Age publishing, a late-20th-century prophecy circuit). None required a hoax to be 'caught' -- the paper trail alone is the tell.

title: Crawford's 1968 Art of Wandjina: repainting can mean a wholly new image, not a touch-up
summary: Ian Crawford's ethnographic survey found that Wandjina repainting is not simple restoration: the Wandjina at Langgi, repainted in 1929, was documented as an entirely new image painted over -- not simply refreshing -- the earlier one, changing form and detail each cycle.

title: Wandjina pigment dating: classic forms may be as young as 1,500 years, layered up to 40 deep
summary: Dating of pigment from classic Wandjina paintings suggests the current style may be no more than about 1,500 years old, though the tradition of painting figures in the same rock shelters likely runs deeper. Cross-sections of individual panels show up to 40 distinct paint layers, consistent with regular seasonal repainting compounding over generations.

title: 1987 Ngarinyin Cultural Continuity Project: a real internal debate over how to repaint
summary: When Ngarinyin custodians led by David Mowaljarlai repainted rock shelters in the Gibb River region in 1987, some rock-art specialists objected that non-traditional materials and participants outside the customary age and gender roles were used. Mowaljarlai's response was that Wandjina images are not 'art' and so outside aesthetic critique -- a genuine, unresolved disagreement about what counts as authentic renewal.

title: 2011 Perth Wandjina graffiti sparked backlash from the culture that owns the imagery
summary: When Wandjina imagery appeared as unauthorized street art around Perth in 2011, Aboriginal community members objected -- not as a debate over accuracy, but over who has standing to reproduce a living sacred image at all, reinforcing that this is treated as owned cultural property, not open folklore.

title: The real Wandjina controversy is internal, and it is not about aliens
summary: Round 1 found the alien reading is an outsider projection the culture rejects outright. The deeper, live disagreement documented here is entirely internal: who may repaint, with what materials, and by whose authority -- a genuine unresolved question inside a genuinely living tradition, which the alien framing never engages with at all.

title: Wandjina: how far back does the underlying motif go, if repainting erases the datable original?
summary: Because each repainting can replace rather than restore the layer beneath it, pigment dating on a visible surface only ever dates the most recent cycle. Without a shelter where an original layer survived undisturbed beneath 40-plus later ones, the deep antiquity of the Wandjina motif itself -- as opposed to the current visible style -- may not be answerable by dating alone.

title: The Nazca 'Astronaut': a 30-meter hillside figure, unlike the rest of the geoglyphs
summary: Separate from Nazca's famous animal figures, a roughly 30-meter humanoid on a hillside -- round head, large eyes, an upraised arm -- is visible from ground level rather than only from the air, and is nicknamed the Astronaut, the Owl Man or the Giant.

title: Archaeologists genuinely do not agree on what the Nazca Astronaut depicts
summary: Unlike the broader Nazca lines, where ritual-path and water-shrine theories converge, the Astronaut figure has no consensus reading: proposals include a shaman in trance with arms raised toward the spirit world, a celestial deity, a fisherman holding a net, and a territorial marker. Sources calling it 'one of the most enigmatic and controversial figures' at the site are not being coy -- this one is actually open.

title: Tourism sites call the extraterrestrial reading of the Nazca Astronaut the 'most popular' theory
summary: Several Nazca tourism and pop-history sites present the space-traveler interpretation as the leading explanation for the Astronaut figure's helmet-like round head and raised arm -- flagged, even by those sites, as the speculative option rather than a scholarly finding.

title: The Nazca Astronaut is the honest exception in this whole research program
summary: Every other subject across rounds 1 and 2 has a specific, checkable mainstream answer, even where the alien reading is loud. The Astronaut figure does not: no glyphs name it, no excavated shrine explains it, and the shaman, deity and fisherman theories genuinely compete. If the brief was to hunt honestly for a thin scholarly account, this is it.

title: Nazca Astronaut: what would settle it
summary: The pottery-at-intersections method that supports the ritual-path theory for the rest of Nazca has not been reported specifically at the Astronaut hillside; a targeted excavation there, rather than further stylistic argument, is the kind of evidence that actually moved the broader Nazca debate.

title: Tassili n'Ajjer Round Head chronology: from wild guesses to a real specialist consensus
summary: Early estimates for the Round Head rock-art style of the central Sahara ranged from about 10,000 to over 20,000 years -- dates Jean-Loic Le Quellec calls poorly argued. Alfred Muzzolini's reassessment, refined with cartographic and phylogenetic methods, moved specialists to a much narrower consensus of roughly 7500-5500 BCE, now broadly accepted.

title: The 'Great Martian God' of Sefar was Henri Lhote's own evocative nickname, not a claim
summary: Lhote, who surveyed Tassili n'Ajjer in the 1950s, named the towering, featureless-headed Jabbaren/Sefar figure the 'Great Martian God' as a description of its uncanny appearance. Archaeologists read it, via analogy to later sub-Saharan African ritual practice, as a masked ancestral or ceremonial figure tied to initiation rites.

title: Ancient-astronaut writers read Lhote's 'Great Martian God' nickname as a literal spacesuit claim
summary: Popular ancient-astronaut sources describe the towering, featureless Sefar/Jabbaren figure as depicting gloves, a helmet and a suit resembling modern spacesuits, arguing people would only paint what they directly observed -- treating Lhote's descriptive nickname as though it were physical evidence rather than a caption.

title: Tassili's dating is settled; its meaning still leans entirely on analogy
summary: Even with chronology resolved to roughly 7500-5500 BCE, the identification of the Round Head figures as masked ritual or ancestral beings rests on comparison to sub-Saharan African ethnography recorded thousands of years later and a continent's width away -- a real evidentiary gap, unlike Pacal's named glyphs or Nazca's excavated ritual pottery.

title: Radiating-head iconography arose independently in Egypt, Persia, Greece, India and Buddhist Asia
summary: A luminous or radiating disc around a divine head appears in ancient Egyptian art, in the khvarenah of Zoroastrian Persia associated with Mithra by the 300s BCE, around Helios and Apollo in Greek art, in rayed aureoles on Indus-valley Mohenjo-daro pottery from around 2000 BCE, and in Buddhist art from Gandhara by the 1st century CE -- centuries before it entered Christian art in the 4th century CE.

title: Art historians read the recurring halo as convergent solar symbolism, not one shared image
summary: Rather than one culture copying another in every instance, art historians treat the halo as multiple societies independently reaching for the same visual solution: the sun is the shared, universally intuitive reference for divine radiance, power and holiness, which is why the motif needs no cultural-contact explanation wherever it appears.

title: Lewis-Williams and Dowson's 1988 entoptic model: six geometric shape types tied to trance stages
summary: The Signs of All Times (Current Anthropology, 1988) proposes rock-art motifs across unconnected cultures share a neuropsychological source: geometric forms the human nervous system generates under altered consciousness (grid, lines, dots, zigzags, catenary curves, filigrees), moving through stages from abstract pattern to iconic imagery shaped by each culture's own mythic content.

title: The entoptic model has real critics inside rock-art scholarship, not just cranks
summary: Archaeologist Paul Bahn and psychologist Patricia Helvenston argue that projecting documented modern shamanic practice back tens of thousands of years onto Palaeolithic art is methodologically invalid, and originally questioned whether psychotropic plants were even available. The plant point is now generally considered wrong (native psilocybin species existed); the analogy-across-time point remains a live methodological argument.

title: Two unrelated mainstream frameworks already explain the recurring shapes, without contact
summary: Solar-symbol convergence (halos, radiating heads) and entoptic neurology (geometric trance imagery) are independent lines of argument from different fields, yet both do the same work the ancient-astronaut genre claims only alien contact can do: explain why unconnected ancient cultures produced strikingly similar shapes, using nothing but the shared human body and the shared sky.

title: No published catalog cross-maps this program's depictions against either framework
summary: Solar convergence explains radiating heads and haloes; entoptic neurology explains geometric trance motifs -- but nobody has published a single site-by-site table testing every depiction across rounds 1 and 2 (Val Camonica, Wandjina, Tassili, the Nazca figures, Pacal) against both frameworks at once. That table, not another individual rebuttal, is what would actually close the recurring-shapes question.

title: The recency signature has a canonical name: Hobsbawm and Rangers "invented tradition" (1983)
summary: Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Rangers The Invention of Tradition (Cambridge, 1983) defines exactly the pattern this topic found four times: practices presented as descending from the distant past that are in fact recent, often deliberately constructed, borrowing real ancient materials to lend a novel thing legitimacy. Hobsbawms introduction states that traditions which appear or claim to be old are often quite recent in origin and sometimes invented, and that they surface when an authority faces a new situation. The Blue Star Kachina, Dogon Sirius, the Emerald Tablets and the Kolbrin are not four anomalies -- they are four instances of a category with forty years of historiography behind it.

title: The Blue Star Kachina paper trail, dated: a 1958 roadside conversation, 1959 pamphlets, first print 1980
summary: Round 1 logged that Colavito found no version predating the late 20th century. The chronology is sharper. Methodist pastor David Young picked up a Hopi hitchhiker calling himself White Feather in 1958 and wrote a pamphlet from memory; pamphlets circulated from 1959; the NAME Blue Star Kachina appears in no source before Frank Waters Book of the Hopi (1963); the earliest printed text of the nine signs Colavito could locate is Jochmans Rolling Thunder: The Coming Earth Changes (1980). Colavito on Youngs role: the Christian apocalyptic themes make plain he was likely far more than the mere transmitter. Hopi elders decried the 1987 gathering at Prophecy Rock; no Hopi took part.
